clue.text: Type of 22 with forehead wrinkled by nods, lies 25 10

definitions.note: the definition describes the subject of the old song, who lies mouldering in the grave

parts.note: a john, or apple-john, is an old variety of apple, so a type of apple tree's fruit
the brow is the forehead

indicators.note: wrinkled says the words by nods are crumpled into a new order

explanation.surface: A gardener describes some apple variety with a furrowed brow, nodding off and lying in the grave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrinkled' scrambles the two words that follow it. 25 10 points to the song's opening line, where the body lies a-mouldering in the grave; an apple-john is an old keeping apple.
explanation.definitionFit: The marching song opens by saying the abolitionist's corpse lies mouldering in the grave, so the definition paraphrases its first line.

clue.text: Confederate leader jives wildly about and offers change

indicators.note: about says one rearranged group goes round the other
wildly says the letters of jives are thrown into disorder
change says the letters of and offers are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Southern general dances wildly and proposes reform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wildly' turns JIVES into JE...VIS, which goes 'about' FFERSONDA, the anagram (from 'change') of AND OFFERS.
explanation.definitionFit: He was president of the Confederate States during the American Civil War, its political leader.

clue.text: Unlike 1 across, show dislike of dreadful monologues about acting as bridge?

parts.note: to hiss is to show disapproval, as an audience does

explanation.surface: An audience hisses at awful speeches about bridges.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dreadful' scrambles the speeches, which go 'about' the bridge's action. In the song the body stays in the grave while the soul keeps going, hence 'Unlike 1 across'.
explanation.definitionFit: The body lies still in its grave but the spirit, in the song's chorus, keeps advancing: the contrast the definition draws.

clue.text: Try m-mouth coming up with the French for plant

indicators.note: in a down entry coming up means the pieces are read from the bottom upwards

a stammered M before mouth, which is GOB in slang

explanation.surface: Someone stammers about a mouth while trying out French words for a plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming up' turns the stammered try-mouth upwards in this down entry; gob is British slang for mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: Bog myrtle, or sweet gale, is an aromatic shrub of wet moorland, so it is a plant.

clue.text: Objection with 13 — Scottish port sold out

definitions.note: 13 is the puzzle's word for an answer to a problem; objection and answer together name an old method of debate

indicators.note: out says the letters of sold are put out of order

explanation.surface: A Scottish harbour town has sold out, prompting objections.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' scrambles 'sold'. The phrase is an old Scots term for disputation by objection and solution, listed in Chambers.
explanation.definitionFit: Ob and sol is an abbreviated form of objection and solution, the formal back-and-forth of scholastic argument.

clue.text: End in a novel writer's name

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters of end in a take a fresh order

explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like the book in which the end comes; it rearranges END IN A. The writer is Nadine Gordimer.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the first name of the South African novelist Gordimer, so a writer's name.

clue.text: Initiate request at home

parts.note: to beg is to ask for something
in means at home

clue.text: Some bones in the face need oxygen on top

indicators.note: in says one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: a dial is the face of a clock or watch

explanation.definitionFit: A diabolo is a toy spinning top, a two-headed spool whirled on a string between two sticks.

clue.text: Guardian's road to knowledge: utter at speed in London area

parts.note: a newspaper's editorial voice is we, so the Guardian's own word for itself
St is short for street
ken is knowledge, as in beyond one's ken

explanation.surface: A newspaper's route to learning is to speak fast.
explanation.walkthrough: A ton is British slang for 100 mph; WEST KENSINGTON is a district of west London.
explanation.definitionFit: West Kensington is a district of west London, so it names an area of the city.

clue.text: Angle for distribution of a drug by ferry here?

explanation.definitionFit: Fishguard in Pembrokeshire is a ferry terminal for sailings to Rosslare, so ferries come and go there.

clue.text: See 25
Point to thin hardwood

parts.note: E, east, is a compass point
bony means skinny

explanation.surface: A carpenter gestures towards a slim piece of hardwood.
explanation.definitionFit: Ebony is a dense dark timber from tropical trees, a classic hardwood.

clue.text: Row at home — complaint — going to restaurant

parts.note: a din is a loud noise, a row
in means at home
gout is an ailment, a complaint

explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' rhymes with cow here, a noise, though it reads as a quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: Dining out means eating a meal away from home, typically at a restaurant.

clue.text: Not the dry part of the puzzle

definitions.text: Not the dry part of the puzzle

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a liquid with something dissolved in it and the answer that resolves a puzzle.

clue.text: Refined ordinary language — 1 across didn't!

parts.note: U means upper-class, refined, in Nancy Mitford's U and non-U
prose is ordinary written language as opposed to verse

explanation.surface: Polished everyday speech is something the corpse in the song never managed.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class comes from a 1950s British debate on posh and common usage.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic past tense of uprise means got up; the body in the song stayed put in its grave.

clue.text: Baroque composer for piano consequently lies hammered

ergo is Latin for therefore

indicators.note: hammered says the letters of lies are beaten into a new shape

explanation.surface: A pianist bangs away at a Baroque piece, telling lies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hammered' scrambles 'lies' to finish the name, after the musical marking and the Latin for therefore.
explanation.definitionFit: Giovanni Battista Pergolesi was an Italian composer of the early eighteenth century, the late Baroque era.

clue.text: Row, perhaps, over movement of that building

parts.note: of that building is possessive, the dome's, perhaps alluding to the Millennium Dome
a tic is an involuntary movement

explanation.surface: An argument erupts over a building's move.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' places DOME'S above TIC in the down entry. The Millennium Dome, a much-disputed London building, explains 'that'.

clue.text: Colours may be and lie maybe, with small child (male, nuts)

explanation.definitionFit: A ship's flag nailed to the mast cannot be struck, so the idiom means committed and refusing to give in.

clue.text: 16 animal breaking into secret

explanation.definitionFit: In petto, Italian for in one's breast, describes something kept private, as a pope's unannounced cardinals.

clue.text: Denomination of contract, other than Bottom's

parts.note: not means other than
read as bottoms, plural of a person's rear, which are rumps

explanation.definitionFit: In bridge the contract names a suit or no trumps, its denomination, so the phrase is one possible denomination.
